analysis.title: FICC Weekly - UK Labour Mkt Data + CPI, Japan GDP + CPI, FOMC Minutes
key_insights: Mizuho says global rates are driven by the Fed regime, not by oil or the AI story. The rates-oil correlation turned modestly positive over the past week but flips too often to be structural.

The AI-related bid for duration has produced a bull-flattening bias over the last five weeks. Mizuho says this is not evidence the US economy is rolling over: GDP grew 3.4% annualised last quarter, payrolls have strengthened and inflation is above target.
Much of the rally came through lower oil prices and inflation expectations, not a collapse in real yields. US gasoline is about $4.07 nationally, roughly 40 cents below late-September levels.
The energy shock is expected to feed through with a lag into Q4 and 2027 via logistics costs and services inflation. Mizuho says it is more likely to reinforce the Fed regime than replace it.
Hyperscalers prefer long-tenor issuance and now hold almost 30% of IG 30-year market share. Together with data-centre financing needs, Mizuho sees this as a future catalyst for US curve steepening.
All four major central banks are being pushed the same way by the energy shock, which limits policy divergence. Mizuho still favours UK flatteners versus US steepeners over the medium term.
UK labour-market quantities point to meaningful slack: unemployment is 4.7% against a five-year average of about 4.4%, and the vacancy-to-unemployment ratio is 0.4x against 0.6-1.0x in 2022-23.
UK wages are stickier than slack implies, especially regular private-sector AWE pay. This keeps the BoE concerned about second-round effects.
Markets price about a 76% probability of a December BoE hike (almost 20bp) and about four further hikes through 2027. Bailey said another hike is 'more likely than not' if the Iran conflict persists.
UK October CPI is expected at 3.6% YoY headline and 2.8% core. Mizuho says services CPI is the bigger wild card for policy beyond December.
Softer UK labour and CPI data has more room to push GBP yields lower, given how hawkish the pricing already is, especially the pace of hikes after December.
Mizuho sees the Nvidia reaction as buy-the-fact and does not read much into it. The wider concern is AI-sector interlinkages flagged by the IMF and BIS in October.
An AI slowdown could weaken Japan's exports, earnings and wages and make the BoJ more cautious, so an AI risk-off move may not produce straightforward JPY strength.

Japanese officials stepped up verbal intervention as USD/JPY neared and briefly passed 160. Mimura said recent moves were 'too rapid' and referred to the coordinated Japan-US intervention of late July (July 31).

Mizuho says verbal warnings or intervention may not reverse the yen's decline while US-Japan policy divergence persists beyond the expected December BoJ hike. Whether the US would cooperate again after the midterms is an open question.

Japan's July-Sep GDP is due Monday 16 November and could be negative, with real consumption down 6.8% YoY in September. Trade data is due the 18th and nationwide CPI on the 20th. Hawkish BoJ member Takata speaks on the 16th, and the linker and 20-year JGB auctions are also due.
earnings_insights: Nvidia's post-earnings move is read as a buy-the-fact reaction, with no company-specific implication drawn. No EPS or revenue figures are given.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Growth does not indicate the US economy is rolling over, despite the AI-driven rally in duration.
About 40 cents below late-September levels, which helped lower inflation expectations.
Both the market and the BoE expect inflation momentum to continue, driven by energy and the Ofgem price-cap increase.
Expected unchanged. Services CPI is the swing factor for the BoE beyond December.
Above the five-year average of about 4.4%, which signals labour slack.
Four vacancies per ten unemployed workers, well below 2022-23 levels, which signals slack.
Market pricing is already hawkish, so softer data has more scope to challenge it.
Likely to weigh on Q3 GDP through weaker private consumption.
AI-related exports and investment may keep growth positive, but the outlook is uncertain.

trade_ideas.description: Medium-term UK flatteners versus US steepeners
trade_ideas.rationale: All four major central banks face the same energy shock, which limits divergence. The UK curve is expected to flatten on hikes, while US long-end supply from AI-related issuance steepens the US curve.

risk_factors: Renewed rises in oil or gas prices would raise the probability of a December BoE hike.
Second-round effects of the energy shock on wages and services inflation, with clearer evidence possibly only from spring 2027 (Pill).
Weaker AI investment and earnings, with leverage and interlinkages amplifying the adjustment (IMF and BIS warnings).
AI hyperscaler long-tenor issuance and data-centre financing adding long-end Treasury supply.
Yen depreciation past 160 prompting intervention, and uncertain US cooperation.
Weak Japanese consumption and a possibly negative Q3 GDP print.
geopolitical: US-Iran conflict: deal/no-deal headlines move oil one day and not the next, and renewed strikes suggest the conflict could last at least another week.
Qatar buying US LNG and the UAE building bypass pipelines are cited as adaptation that limits the oil shock.
Japan-US coordinated yen intervention on July 31, and whether the US would cooperate again after the midterm elections.
Japan's possible response to USD/JPY near 160, and the IMF 'free floating' regime classification (no more than three intervention episodes in six months).

tension_points.theme: UK wage stickiness vs labour slack
tension_points.bull_case: Sticky wages and energy-driven inflation keep the BoE hiking, with a December hike and about four more through 2027 priced.
tension_points.bear_case: Quantity-based slack measures (unemployment 4.7%, vacancy ratio 0.4x) suggest wages should cool, so softer data could push GBP yields lower and challenge hike pricing.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Next week's UK labour and CPI releases, notably services CPI and private-sector AWE growth, showing slack feeding through to wages.

tension_points.bull_case: Verbal intervention and the memory of July's coordinated action could slow yen weakness near 160.
tension_points.bear_case: Intervention may not reverse the trend while US-Japan policy divergence persists beyond December.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A coordinated Japan-US intervention, or a narrowing of the policy-rate differential after the December FOMC and BoJ meetings.
